title: San Francisco’s Local-Wine Complex
summary:
San Francisco and its immediate surrounds have never been more packed with places where a thirsty wine lover can sit

The post San Francisco’s Local-Wine Complex appeared first on Vinography.
content:
San Francisco and its immediate surrounds have never been more packed with places where a thirsty wine lover can sit down to a great glass of wine. Almost 20 years ago, I started keeping track of local wine bars, of which there were only a handful. Since then, that number has exploded to more than 60, and there are roughly 4,000 restaurants now. And, as the lean years of the pandemic fade into the rear-view mirror, wine lists are again showing variety and heft.

Even so, San Francisco proves to be something of a conundrum for those who wish to drink local. In a region known for all but inventing the farm-to-table dining movement in the US, the locavore ethos has curiously never managed to pervade the wine-drinking culture.

Nearly every wine list in the city will have some California wine on it, but only a few venues seem dedicated to featuring local wine. Instead, most lists mirror the city’s famously cosmopolitan qualities, offering amazing things to drink from the world’s best- (and least-) known wine regions, with only a small percentage (usually 5–15% of the wines on offer) from California. These lists are a delight for both the curious and the discerning wine lover, but they ultimately come at the expense of showcasing and supporting California’s thousands of wineries.

The first part of my monthly column for Jancis Robinson’s website has been made free to read this month, so read the full article introduction here.

The article is followed by my list of the best places to drink California wine in San Francisco, which is only available to subscribers.

My monthly column at JancisRobinson.Com, is available only to subscribers of her website. If you’re not familiar with the site, I urge you to give it a try. It’s only $135 a year (25% off for the holidays!), and well worth the cost, especially considering you basically get free, searchable access to the Oxford Companion to Wine ($65) and maps from the World Atlas of Wine ($50) as part of the subscription costs. Click here to sign up.

Hello and welcome to my weekly roundup of the wine stories that I find of interest on the web. I

content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly roundup of the wine stories that I find of interest on the web. I spend each week exploring the internet for everything published about wine online, and here’s all the stuff that I think would be worth your valuable time.

What the Land Becomes Next
Required reading about Napa.

In praise of (some) old California reds
Jancis raids some cellars.

The Most Bizarre Tale in the History of Oregon Wine
Helluva story. Fascinating.

When Local Laws Threaten a Winery’s Bottom Line
Much reform needed.

WASP – Alentejo’s sustainability programme
EVERY wine region should do this.

Altaya and now much more
Jancis profiles Paulo Pong.

Nasty Not Nice
Well, that’s one proposal. Margaret Rand gets satirical. I think?

California winemaking pioneer Jim Concannon dies at 95
RIP to one of the pioneers.

The Wine Business Needs to Wake Up
Gary Vee is always good for some straight, expletive-laced, talk.

Coping with Compacted Vintages
Some vintages are getting compacted, but others are merely shifting.

Learning the Long Game
Molesworth looks back on his time.

This Obscure Italian Wine From Sonocaia Estate Is Sonoma’s Best-Kept Secret
The secret of Sonoma Sagrantino.

Why drinks brands need to rethink the rules of drinking
Changing times.

The Real Housewives of Conspicuous Consumption
Signaling. It’s all signaling.

A Sonoma Grillo—Wait, What’s a Grillo?
Grillo is not that obscure.

Champagne Ditches Expansion Plans
They’ve talked and talked about it, and now they’re killing the idea.

Loire the New Bordeaux Says Climate Expert
Turn and face the strange

White Wine Finds Its Place in China, From Seafood Stalls to Wine Bars
The only place in the world outside of Europe that drinks Riesling.

A Conversation With Louisa Sawyer Lindquist
One of CA’s best.

An Inspiration From Burgundy Led to the Modern Napa
A nice profile.

‘I lost my entire export business overnight’: the toll of Trump’s tariffs on US wine
Many baskets with many eggs are suffering.

Is this France’s best-value red wine?
A good candidate for sure.

How a Self-Taught Sommelier Became the Best in the American South
Anointed by Michelin.

‘Africa is hot right now’: does the continent hold the key to wine’s recovery?
Insights on the wine scene in Kenya.

Why Crete’s wines and producers are Greece’s best kept secrets
It’s all about the Dafnia.

The Wine World is Finding A New Groove — With a Little Help From Hip-Hop
A nice profile of Milena Berman.

Gallo’s Winery Closures Reveal What Customers Want Beyond the Product
The business magazines weigh in on the sitch.

As the Wine Industry Retracts, Some Are Still Betting Big on Napa
There’s always someone willing to buy low. It helps if you’re filthy rich.

‘We built this land’: descendants of enslaved people are reclaiming their history across South Africa’s vineyards
What not burying the truth looks like.

Europe is slowly embracing wine in pouches instead of bottles. Is America next?
Bring it on!

Older Generations Still Thirsty for Wine
A false hope.

title: S.O.R.B.E.T Wine Tasting: Nov 8, San Francisco
summary:
I don’t know about you, but I love me a good acronym. S.O.R.B.E.T stands for Sonoma Organic Regenerative Biodynamic Educational

The post S.O.R.B.E.T Wine Tasting: Nov 8, San Francisco appeared first on Vinography.
content:
I don’t know about you, but I love me a good acronym. S.O.R.B.E.T stands for Sonoma Organic Regenerative Biodynamic Educational Tasting, and it’s put on by a group of like-minded Sonoma winemakers and winegrowers who have gotten together to highlight their county’s progress towards more ecologically minded ways of farming and winemaking in an era where greenwashing is also on the rise. These are producers who are not just farming organically but are sequestering carbon, capturing runoff, preventing erosion, improving ecology, and supporting communities of people.

Organized by three school friends in the wine business—Morgan Twain-Peterson of Bedrock Wine Co., Katie Bundschu of Gundlach Bundschu, and Sam Coturri of Winery Sixteen600—this event brings together a group of extremely high-integrity wine producers for a walk-around tasting of some really excellent wine.

The list of producers pouring includes: Abbot’s Passage, Bedrock Vineyard, Bedrock Wine Co, Benziger Family Winery, Brown Estate, BUCKLIN, Canihan Family Winery, Dane Cellars, Donum Estate, Enterprise Vineyards, Fest Wine Co., Fresh Wine Co, Gloria Ferrer, Gundlach Bundschu, Hamel Family Wine, Hanzell, Hill of Tara Winery, Kamen Estate Wines, Kivelstadt Cellars, KORBIN KAMERON, Jambe de Bois, Las Vivas, Lasseter Family Winery, Laurel Glen Vineyard, Marioni Wine, Montecillo Vineyard, Once & Future Wine, Pangloss Cellars, Ram’s Gate Winery, Rossi Ranch, Stone Edge Farm Estate Vineyards & Winery, Tidings, Winery Sixteen 600

This will be a delicious way to spend an afternoon, I promise.

2026 Sonoma Organic Regenerative Biodynamic Educational Tasting
Sunday, November 8 – 1:00 PM to 4:00 PM
Fort Mason Center, Gallery 308
2 Marina Boulevard
San Francisco, CA 94123 (map)

Tickets to the event will run you $78.30, and should be purchased in advance online. My advice? Get a good night’s sleep, grab a big lunch ahead of time, and spit so you can try a lot of stuff and still keep your head.

title: Vinography Unboxed: Week of 10/18/26
summary:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep, asking

The post Vinography Unboxed: Week of 10/18/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep, asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This week included a new sparkling wine from the folks at Jackson Family Wines, who have been investing heavily in Oregon in recent years. This new project, Banke Wines, is named after the company’s CEO, Barbara Banke, who swears that she didn’t choose the name for this new line of sparkling wines. The Blanc de Blancs they sent me recently was impeccably made and offered a wonderfully brilliant lemony zing in the glass with just the right balance between fruity freshness and the patina you can get with long lees aging in the bottle. I highly recommend it.

Erica Orr worked as a lab tech at UCSF Hospital in San Francisco, but then a chance meeting with winemaker Aaron Pott at a bar in San Francisco led her down the rabbit hole of winemaking. A bunch of internships, a master’s degree, and years as a consulting enologist later, Erica is making her own wines in Washington State. Her old-vine Chenin Blanc and Salumeria Blend red wines are both very drinkable and tasty, not to mention affordable.

Girard Winery is a brand brought back to life in Napa. Originally a family-owned winery based in Oakville, the physical winery and brand were sold in 1996 to Leslie Rudd, who turned it into Rudd Estate. The Girard brand was purchased from Rudd by Pat Roney in 2000, who made wine under that name even as Roney combined it with Windsor Vineyards to create the company Vintage Wine Estates, which went on to acquire a number of other brands. VWE went bankrupt in 2024, and a number of its brands, including Girard and Clos Pegase, were purchased by Jay Adair, who has pulled them together under the banner of Adair Family Wines. I’m recommending three Girard wines this week: their bright Sauvignon Blanc and their rich and dark Charbono and Mixed Blacks red blend.

Hensel West is a new wine project by Will and Amanda Phelps. Will, of course, is the third generation of the Phelps Family making wine in Napa, after his pioneering grandfather Joseph Phelps established his namesake winery in 1973. To make their wines, Will and Amanda have hired winemaker Ashley Hepworth, who spent 15 years making the wines at Joseph Phelps. They sent through their inaugural bottlings of Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah, and a Bordeaux-style blend for me to try this week. They’re all solid, but the red blend is a standout, offering a refined texture and a nicely restrained expression of fruit. The winery is aiming for a luxury positioning, and all the wines are allocated straight out of the gate, apparently. But if you’re in the market for pricey Napa wines, this is one to keep an eye on.

Notes on all these below.

Tasting Notes

NV Banke “Blanc de Blancs” Chardonnay, Willamette Valley, Oregon
Pale gold in the glass with medium-fine bubbles, this wine smells of freshly cut apples, sea air, and lemon peel. In the mouth, a soft mousse delivers flavors of lemon peel, lemon oil, pomelo, and oyster shells as fantastic acidity makes the mouth water. There’s a hint of salinity here that adds to the overall very delicious package. A whisper of vanilla and crushed nuts lingers in the finish. Barrel-fermented. Spent 47 months on the lees in the bottle before disgorgement in August 2026. 6.5 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. LIVE-certified sustainable. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $70.

2025 Orr “Old Vine” Chenin Blanc, Columbia Valley, Washington
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear and candied ginger. In the mouth, pear and ginger flavors mix with white flowers and a hint of citrus pith. There’s a faint lanolin note that also lingers in the finish. Decent acidity, but I would like more. Fermented with ambient yeasts in old oak barrels and steel drums. Bentonite-fined and sterile-filtered before bottling. 12% alcohol. 386 cases made. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $28. click to buy.

2025 Girard Sauvignon Blanc, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Palest gold in the glass, near colorless, this wine smells of green apples and passionfruit. In the mouth, green apple, passionfruit, and a hint of green bell pepper have a nice brightness thanks to decent acidity. Fermented with ambient yeasts in stainless steel. Malolactic inhibited. 14.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $21. click to buy.

2025 Hensel West “Riverbound Vineyard” Sauvignon Blanc, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Palest greenish-gold in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers, oak, and apples. In the mouth, bright, juicy acidity makes flavors of lemon pith, unripe apple, and crushed nuts quite mouthwatering. The oak is a definite presence here and has the effect of compressing the wine at this point in its evolution, giving an overall impression of narrowness. 14% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $65.

2024 Orr “Salumeria Blend” Red Blend, Columbia Valley, Washington
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of cherries, sour cherries, and a hint of cocoa powder. In the mouth, cherry, cocoa powder, sawdust, and a touch of dried herbs are wrapped in faint gauzy tannins. Decent acidity. A blend of 58% Sangiovese, 37% Cabernet Sauvignon, and 5% Merlot. Aged in old French oak for 10 months. Bottled unfined and unfiltered. 14.1% alcohol. 190 cases made. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $30. click to buy.

2022 Girard Charbono, Calistoga, Napa, California
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of blueberries, woodsmoke, espresso, and licorice. In the mouth, blueberries, licorice, and a smoky blackberry flavor are all wrapped in fine tannins. Decent acidity. Notes of oak and dark berries linger in the finish.13.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $75.

2022 Girard “Mixed Blacks” Red Blend, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of blackberries, earth, licorice, and espresso. In the mouth, sweet oak and espresso notes mix with blackberry and black cherry flavors as fleecy tannins coat the mouth. Heavily oak-inflected, but with enough acidity to keep things fresh. 14.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $70.

2024 Hensel West “Hyde Vineyard” Syrah, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of blueberries, black cherries, and licorice. In the mouth, black cherry and blueberry flavors are smooth and taut across the palate, with fine, powdery tannins and decent acidity. There’s a faint stoniness to the wine, but I would love some more acidity. 14.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $110.

2024 Hensel West “HWX” Red Blend, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in color, this wine smells of black cherry, tobacco, and espresso. In the mouth, fine-grained micro-fleece tannins surround a core of black cherry, blackberry, and espresso notes. Very good acidity. Hold for 3-7 years for best results. A blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, and Petit Verdot aged in 80% new French oak for 19 months.14% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $200.

title: California Cult Bubbles and More: The Latest from Ultramarine & Cruse Wine Co.
summary:
If there were a competition for California’s geekiest winemaker, I’m sure Michael Cruse would make the final round. His willingness

The post California Cult Bubbles and More: The Latest from Ultramarine & Cruse Wine Co. appeared first on Vinography.
content:
If there were a competition for California’s geekiest winemaker, I’m sure Michael Cruse would make the final round. His willingness to dive into the minutiae of (mostly sparkling) winemaking is unparalleled in my experience, something I’m reminded of when I show up to taste at his office, where a 4-foot-by-6-foot poster charting all the metabolic pathways known to science occupies almost the entirety of one wall. I’ll never forget the story he once told me of trying to culture his own yeast and making one of the biggest messes of his life.

The 46-year-old Cruse grew up in San Francisco and later moved to Petaluma. After studying molecular biology at UC Berkeley, Cruse worked in academic labs until he realized that he wasn’t feeding his soul. Inspired by a winemaker’s guest lecture during his college years, he tried his hand in the wine industry, first in enology labs and then in cellars, where he found his true calling.

After working his way up to Associate Winemaker at Merryvale’s Starmont winery in Napa, Cruse struck out on his own, opening a custom crush facility in Petaluma where he could make his own wines.

Along the way, he talked his way into getting some fruit from the legendary Heintz Vineyard on the Sonoma Coast and launched California’s first serious single-vineyard, extended-tirage sparkling wine brand known as Ultramarine. I’ve written in depth about the phenomenon that is Ultramarine before here on Vinography.

In addition to Ultramarine, which is made in such tiny quantities that it couldn’t really sustain a career or a household, Cruse makes a line of wines under the Cruse Wine Co. label that includes pét-nats, sparkling wines, and still red and white wines. The wines range from single-vineyard expressions to California-appellation blends of fruit from various sources. These wines have been designed from the start to be affordable and approachable.

“I was becoming ossified in Napa,” says Cruse about his career before deciding to start his own brand. “I was on the path to make $150 to $200 bottles, and it was bumming me out. With Cruse [Wine Co.], it was always going to be about making wines that people would drink.”

To that end, says Cruse, he hasn’t raised prices on his eponymous wines in 10 years. Ultramarine, too, remains relatively affordable to those on the mailing list, having risen from $45 to $80 or $95 a bottle over the course of 11 vintages. Of course, it trades at much higher prices on the secondary market thanks to its scarcity and high demand.

As top cuvées from some sparkling wine producers in California approach $200, Cruse’s wines, especially those made under the Cruse Wine Co. brand, begin to look like serious bargains. Affordability aside, Cruse has strong opinions about the correct approach to making sparkling wine in California.

“How should we be talking about California sparkling wine?” says Cruse. “This is one of the questions I have. It seems to me that instead of being afraid of sunshine, or overly indulgent, we can have density and weight that feel ripe but not overly fruity, which is where oxidation can come in.”

There are several points in the sparkling winemaking process where oxidation can play a positive role in shaping the character of the wine, but the three primary ones are how the juice is handled prior to and during the fermentation, how the still wine is aged prior to the secondary fermentation in the bottle, and the introduction of older, reserve wine into the overall blend.

Cruz presses slowly, allowing the juice longer contact with oxygen, and opting to ferment in barrels without adding sulfur dioxide continues that oxidative approach. The wines are then aged in barrels for a time with sulfur added to prevent malolactic fermentation, but the barrels allow further micro-oxygenation of the still wines. Finally, perpetual reserves (as Cruse uses with his “Tradition” sparkling wine) can hold a decade or more of older vintages and add further oxidative patina to balance out ripe fruit.

I do find Cruse’s sparkling wines, both those made under the Cruse label and Ultramarine, to be wonderfully balanced between fruit and more savory characteristics, though an extra edge and precision (perhaps thanks to the single-vineyard sourcing) give the Ultramarine wines a fineness that separates them from the Cruse bottlings.

Cruse does many things well when it comes to winemaking, but I particularly admire his attention to acidity. This goes especially for his still wines, which are often overlooked given his talents with bubbles. He’s particularly enamored with the Valdiguié grape variety, which has a long history in California. Long known in California as Napa Gamay, until ampelographers set the record straight, Valdiguié has many charms, not the least of which is a vibrant, juicy acidity accompanying a floral and berry flavor profile.

“It’s one of my favorite wines,” says Cruse, “but I can’t sell it to save my life.”

The Valdiguié and its sibling, the extremely quaffable Monkey Jacket, are, in my opinion, two of California’s better wine values, but they seem destined to remain in the shadow of the sparkling wines that have rightfully made Cruse so well known.

That’s something of a shame. For all his fascination with yeast metabolism and the esoterica of Champagne press cycles, Cruse is really after something pretty simple: wines people want to open on a weekday night. The science is just how he gets there. And since he’s taken care of all that geeky stuff for us, all we have to do is pull the cork.

Tasting Notes

2023 Cruse Wine Co. “Ricci Vineyard Pet Nat” Rosé of Saint Laurent, Los Carneros, Sonoma, California
Light coppery pink in the glass with extremely fine bubbles, this wine smells of peaches, orange creamsicle, and wet pavement. In the mouth, a soft mousse delivers flavors of bubble gum, stone fruit, plum, and citrus peel. Macerated for a few hours, pressed to bottling at 1-1.5 brix, with only the first gentle press fractions used (cuvée only, no taille). Spends 18 months in bottle and is sold undisgorged under a crown cap in pétillant naturel style. 11% alcohol. 4000 bottles made. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $36. click to buy.

2025 Cruse Wine Co. “Deming Pet Nat” Rosé of Valdiguié, Calistoga, Napa, California
Pale gold with a hint of peach and faint tiny bubbles, this wine smells of orange pith, unripe apricot, and a touch of pastry cream. In the mouth, a soft mousse delivers faintly sweet flavors of orange peel, white peach, berries, and a touch of dry herbs. Pretty and refreshing. Dry-farmed, organic 80+ year-old vines. Macerated for a few hours, pressed to bottling at 1-1.5 brix, with only the first gentle press fractions used (cuvée only, no taille). Spends 18 months in the bottle and is sold undisgorged under a crown cap in pétillant naturel style. 12% alcohol. 3500 bottles. Score: around 9. Cost: $35. click to buy.

NV Cruse Wine Co. “Tradition” Rosé Sparkling Wine, California
Light coppery peach in color with very fine bubbles, this wine smells of crabapples, warm wool, dried herbs, and dried flowers. In the mouth, a voluminous, silky mousse delivers flavors of orange peel, berries, a touch of crabapple, and a nice floral aromatic sweetness across the palate. Sophisticated and sensual, with great acidity, lift, and length on the palate. Extremely tasty. 95% Pinot Noir, 5% Chardonnay. Spends 36 months on the lees and receives 6 g/L dosage. All 2021 fruit. 12.5% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $60. click to buy.

NV Cruse Wine Co. “Tradition” Sparkling Wine, California
Light gold in the glass with a hint of bronze and fine bubbles, this wine smells of marzipan, biscotti, and roasted nuts. In the mouth, a silky, voluminous mousse delivers dried orange peel, roasted sesame and poppy seeds, savory dried herbs, and a touch of nougat. Long on the palate with a lovely energy and a mysterious aspect. Wonderfully delicious. A blend of 57% Pinot and 43% Chardonnay. Two-thirds of the juice comes from 2022 fruit, the remainder being a perpetual cuvée going back to 2015. Ages for 30 months on the lees in the bottle before being disgorged in January of 2026 with zero dosage.12.5% alcohol. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $50. click to buy.

2021 Cruse Wine Co. “Blanc de Noirs” Sparkling Wine, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Pale gold in the glass with very fine bubbles, this wine smells of crushed cashews, white flowers, and resinous herbs. In the mouth, salty crushed nuts, rosemary, bitter herbs, and wet chalkboard take on a chalky texture through the finish. Great acidity and lovely salinity. A radically distinctive and unusual wine. Some extra Pinot Noir fruit from Charlie Heintz became available, and the puncheons where the finished wine was aged were hard-bunged, taped, and not topped up, allowing some of them to form a blanket of flor yeast. The puncheons that didn’t get flor were moved into the rosé program. The wine was then aged for 30 months on the lees in bottle before disgorgement with zero dosage. 12.5% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $60.

2024 Cruse Wine Co. “Rorick Vineyard” Chardonnay, Sierra Foothills, California
Pale yellow-gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon blossom, candied lemon peel, and a hint of candle wax. In the mouth, silky flavors of lemon oil, lemon peel, and white flowers have a more delicate acidity and a faint stony minerality. Vines were planted in the late 1970s and are own-rooted, growing in mica-schist soils. Whole cluster pressed. 13.5% alcohol. 450 cases made. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $32. click to buy.

2023 Cruse Wine Co. “Rancho Chimiles” Valdiguié, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Medium purple in the glass, this wine smells of boysenberries and blueberries. In the mouth, stony and crunchy blueberry and boysenberry flavors are mixed with dried herbs and bright floral notes. Faint tannins have an amazing stony grip. Fantastic acidity and a sort-of-stony seamlessness that is quite alluring. Vines planted in the early 1970s. Fully destemmed and fermented in concrete, where it ages for 12 months before bottling. 12% alcohol. 275 cases made. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $33. click to buy.

2023 Cruse Wine Co. “Monkey Jacket” Red Blend, California
Medium garnet in the glass with purple highlights, this wine smells of boysenberries, blackberries, and dried herbs. In the mouth, boysenberries, licorice, charred vegetables, and dried herbs. Powdery tannins stiffen slightly, with excellent acidity keeping things fresh. Notes of purple SweetTarts linger in the finish. An equal blend of Valdiguié, Petite Sirah, Carignan, and Zinfandel, with a trace of Tannat, all fermented separately. The Valdiguie and Zinfandel are destemmed, the others with whole clusters. Blended early, and then aged for 12 months in a combination of 50% concrete and 50% neutral wood. 13% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $27. click to buy.

Note that the prices shown below are what the wines can be purchased for on the secondary market.

2021 Ultramarine “Michael Mara Blanc de Blancs” Sparkling Wine, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Pale yellow gold in the glass with fine bubbles, this wine smells of lemon pith, wet chalkboard, and a hint of toasted sesame. In the mouth, toasted sesame and crushed roasted nuts mix with white flowers and stony wet pavement, all borne on a silky, airy, voluminous mousse. Notes of dried herbs and citrus pith linger in the finish along with a hint of sourdough croutons. Long finish. Great poise. There’s a floral aspect that adds an extra allure to this stunning wine. 100% Chardonnay. The still wine spends about a year in 30% new large-format oak before secondary fermentation. Aged for 44 months on the lees in the bottle before disgorging in November 2025 with 2 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. 1200 bottles made. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $190.

2021 Ultramarine “Charles Heintz Blanc de Blancs” Sparkling Wine, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Pale yellow gold in the glass with fine bubbles, this wine smells of salty struck match, charred lemon peel, and a hint of dried herbs. In the mouth, a mousse of moderate volume delivers salty flavors of lemon peel, toasted sourdough, a faint touch of green herbs, and gorgeous stony wet chalkboard minerality. Lemon peel and orange peel flavors linger in the finish with sea air and a touch of kelp. A stunning, electric wine that manages to be generous and electrically lean at the same time. 100% Chardonnay. The still wine spends about a year in 30% new large-format oak before secondary fermentation. Aged for 44 months on the lees in bottle before disgorging in November 2025 with 2 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. 2000 bottles made. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $190. click to buy.

2021 Ultramarine “Charles Heintz Blanc de Noirs” Sparkling Wine, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Pale yellow gold in color with fine bubbles, this wine smells of wet chalkboard and cherries, white flowers, and acerola. In the mouth, a silky, voluminous mousse delivers flavors of acerola, cherry, saline citrus peel, gorgeous wet chalkboard, and a hint of tidepool. Tangy and mouthwatering, with a crazy salty candied citrus note that lingers in the finish for a long time. Simply gorgeous. 100% Pinot Noir. The still wine spends about a year in 30% new large-format oak before secondary fermentation. Aged for 44 months on the lees in bottle before disgorging in November 2025 with 2 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. 1600 bottles made. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $172. click to buy.

2021 Ultramarine “Charles Heintz” Rosé Sparkling Wine, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Light coppery pink with a hint of orange and very fine bubbles, this wine smells of berries and a hint of hibiscus. In the mouth, a softer mousse delivers faint struck match and berry notes, saline with a lovely sea-air quality, and a touch of acerola and citrus peel lingering in the finish. A blend of 50% Pinot Noir, 50% Chardonnay, plus 5-8% still red wine for color. The still wine spends about a year in 30% new large-format oak before secondary fermentation. Aged for 44 months on the lees in bottle before disgorging in November 2025 with 6 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. 4000 bottles made. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $180. click to buy.

2021 Ultramarine “Hirsch Vineyard” Sparkling Rosé of Pinot Noir, Fort Ross-Seaview, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Light coppery pink in the glass with fine bubbles, this wine smells of red apple skin, cranberries, citrus peel, and dried herbs. In the mouth, a softer, silky mousse delivers flavors of strawberry, biscuits, dried herbs, and a hint of crushed nuts. In the finish, there’s a dried herb quality that lingers for a long time. Fantastic. 100% Pinot Noir from Block 15 of Raschen Ridge at Hirsch Vineyards, saignéed after 12 hours of maceration. The still wine spends about a year in 30% new large-format oak before secondary fermentation. Aged for 44 months on the lees in bottle before disgorging in November 2025 with 6 g/L dosage. 12.5% alcohol. 4000 bottles made. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $160. click to buy.

title: Burgundy Comes to SF: Notes from La Paulée de San Francisco
summary:
Opportunities to taste top Burgundy wines in San Francisco are rare and getting rarer. The cost of the wines, the

The post Burgundy Comes to SF: Notes from La Paulée de San Francisco appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Opportunities to taste top Burgundy wines in San Francisco are rare and getting rarer. The cost of the wines, the sometimes shrinking quantities in which they are produced, and the degree to which they really don’t need any promotion to sell amongst the collectors, restaurants, and stores all clamoring for allocations means they generally just aren’t made available for tasting. When they are opened on occasion in tasting formats, the producer is seldom in attendance.

That’s why the Grand Tasting at La Paulée de San Francisco event ends up being such a pleasure. Great wines are opened and available for tasting, usually poured by the vignerons themselves. Glassware is excellent, oysters are being shucked, and everyone seems to delight at the chance to experience wines that are increasingly out of reach. While it is expensive relative to other public tastings, the price ends up being reasonable considering the prices of the wines on offer (but more about that in a moment).

The 2026 edition of the event was held in the beautiful enclosed courtyard at One Sansome Street in the city’s Financial District, and featured a fantastic selection of top names from both the Côte de Beaune and the Côte de Nuits.

Almost all the wines were from the 2023 vintage, which was an unusual one for Burgundy, in that for the first time in a while, the vines were holding a lot of fruit. Yields were up about 30% on average during a year that was overall warmer than average in France but somehow managed to stay relatively chilly in Burgundy. Summer was stormier than normal, followed by a late-season heatwave that rapidly pushed fruit towards ripeness as harvest approached.

The reports I’ve read about the harvest featured a lot of discussion about yield management for quality, with many producers dropping fruit to try to achieve some balance on their vines, and the results of these efforts were mixed, especially in Pinot Noir. Chardonnay seemed better at handling an increased crop load, leading commentators to suggest the vintage was more consistent for white wines than for red.

I don’t taste Burgundy regularly enough or with enough depth to have perspective on it from vintage to vintage, but I can say I found a lot of wines to like among these 2023s. The best were racy, vibrant, and had very fine textures.

The prices for these wines are generally eye-popping. I never thought I’d be one of those old guys saying, “I remember when you could actually afford these wines,” but here I am saying I can almost remember when Burgundy was affordable. These prices? They’re just insane. No reliable relationship exists between price and quality in any way that would be useful to the uninformed consumer – I’ve got $40, $80, and $225 white wines rated the same, and I’ve got $145, $820, and $1200 red wines rated the same. The average price of a white wine below is $225. The average price of a red wine below is $350. The fact that only 4 of the roughly 65 wines rated below can be purchased for under $80 just makes me sad.

These are amazing wines, but that hardly matters when only a tiny fraction of the top 1% of consumers can ever hope to drink them.

Tasting Notes

These tasting notes and scores were all made at a walk-around tasting, which is not the optimal format for evaluating wines. Take the tasting notes and scores below with whatever grain of salt you need to, given those circumstances.

White Wines With a Score Around 9.5

2023 Domaine Fontaine-Gagnard Bâtard-Montrachet Grand Cru, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Near colorless in the glass, this wine smells of wet stones and lemon peel. In the mouth, stony, saline flavors have a crystalline clarity and a long, resonant, cistern-like finish. Fantastic acidity. Scintillating in quality, and utterly compelling. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $445. click to buy.

2023 Domaine François Carillon “Les Aubues” Puligny-Montrachet, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of flowers, wet stones, and lemon oil. In the mouth, bright, saline flavors of lemon oil are shot through with stony minerality as excellent acidity helps notes of salty lemon peel linger for a long while in the finish. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $??

2023 Domaine François Carillon “Les Perrières Premier Cru” Puligny-Montrachet, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Light gold in the glass, this wine smells of flowers, lemon blossom, and wet stones. In the mouth, tangy, saline flavors of lemon oil, lemon peel, and pomelo linger for a long time in the finish. Fantastic acidity and a real stony depth make this a stupendous wine. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $221. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Ponsot “Clos des Monts-Luisants Premier Cru Vieilles Vignes” Aligoté, Morey-Saint-Denis, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of flowers, wet chalkboard, and lemon pith. In the mouth, bright lemon and juicy grapefruit flavors have a stony, saline quality and zippy acidity. Crackling and crunchy with brightness, this is a mouthwatering wine. Vines planted in 1911. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $225. click to buy.

White Wines With a Score Between 9 and 9.5

2023 Domaine Hubert Lamy “Haute Densité” Saint-Aubin, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine has a stony, flinty nose. In the mouth, bright, saline flavors of lemon pith take on a resinous quality as they linger in a long finish. Great acidity and finesse. Planted at a density of 30,000 vines per hectare. Delicious. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $750. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Hubert Lamy “Les Chaumées Premier Cru” Chassagne-Montrachet, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon peel, lemon pith, and wet pavement. In the mouth, delicate floral notes mix with stony, saline flavors that have a crystalline purity, as excellent acidity lets citrus and white flowers linger in the finish. Lovely. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $??

2023 Domaine Fontaine-Gagnard Chassagne-Montrachet, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of flowers and lemon peel with a touch of struck-match reduction. In the mouth, salty flavors of lemon peel, grapefruit, and pomelo have a stony quality, excellent acidity, and wonderful silky texture. Delicious. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $110. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Fontaine-Gagnard “Les Vergers Premier Cru” Chassagne-Montrachet, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Near colorless in the glass, this wine smells of wet stones and struck match. In the mouth, bright, saline flavors of lemon pith and pomelo linger for a very long time in the finish. Cut and well-defined, with excellent acidity and balance. Extremely tasty. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $100. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Fontaine-Gagnard “Les Caillerets Premier Cru” Chassagne-Montrachet, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Near colorless in the glass, this wine smells of resin, flint, and lemon pith. In the mouth, saline flavors of lemon pith and grapefruit have a deeply stony quality that lingers, stony, through a long finish. Excellent acidity and poise. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $160. click to buy.

2023 Domaine François Carillon “Clos du Vieux Château” Puligny-Montrachet, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of candied lemon, vanilla, and resin. In the mouth, tangy flavors of lemon peel and pomelo have a resinous, stony quality as excellent acidity keeps the mouth watering. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $110. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Bachelet-Monnot Chassagne-Montrachet, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of salty lemon pith and wet stones. In the mouth, saline, stony flavors of lemon pith and grapefruit linger in the finish. Great acidity and wonderful texture, with a nice stony cut to the wine. Delicious. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $125. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Pierre Morey “Les Tessons” Meursault, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of flint and struck match, lemon pith, and grapefruit. In the mouth, zingy grapefruit flavors are backed by great acidity and a long finish. Mouthwatering and delicious. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $200. click to buy.

White Wines With a Score Around 9

2023 Domaine Hubert Lamy “Clos de la Chatenière Premier Cru” Saint-Aubin, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of struck match and wet stones. In the mouth, flavors of lemon pith, grapefruit, and wet pavement have a wonderfully stony quality to them, excellent acidity, and a nice long finish. Score: around 9. Cost: $225. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Bachelet-Monnot “La Fussière Premier Cru” Maranges, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of wet stones, lemon pith, and pomelo pith. In the mouth, stony flavors of lemon pith and lemon peel have a faintly resinous edge as well as very good acidity. Nicely balanced. Score: around 9. Cost: $85. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Bachelet-Monnot “Les Folatières Premier Cru” Puligny-Montrachet, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon, oak, and vanilla. In the mouth, flavors of lemon, oak, and lemon peel have a stony undertone and good acidity. A little heavy on the wood here, but very good acidity and nice minerality mean this will likely age well. Score: around 9. Cost: $265. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Pierre Morey Bourgogne Aligoté, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of pithy lemon and grapefruit. In the mouth, flavors of lemon and grapefruit are driven by great acidity over a lean, wet pavement minerality. Score: around 9. Cost: $40. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Clos de la Chapelle “Cuvée Exceptionnelle” Corton-Charlemagne Grand Cru, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of wet stones, lemon pith and coconut. In the mouth, flavors of wet pavement and lemon pith have a stony quality. Very good acidity and less wood on the palate than on the nose. Tasty. Score: around 9. Cost: $??

2023 Pierre Meurgey “Les Bouthières Premier Cru” Pouilly-Fuissé, Mâconnais, Burgundy, France
Pale greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of wet chalkboard, lemon pith, and lemon oil. In the mouth, zingy, tangy flavors have a wet chalkboard minerality. Excellent acidity and a nice, bright, sunny complexion. Score: around 9. Cost: $??

White Wines With a Score Between 8.5 and 9

2023 Domaine Hubert Lamy “En Remilly Premier Cru” Saint-Aubin, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of struck match, wet pavement, and lemon pith. In the mouth, saline, stony flavors of lemon pith have very good acidity. Notes of citrus linger through the finish. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $260. click to buy.

2023 Domaine François Carillon Puligny-Montrachet, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of grapefruit and flowers. In the mouth, floral and vanilla flavors have a silky texture and very good acidity. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $160. click to buy.

2023 Pierre Meurgey Corton-Charlemagne Grand Cru, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon curd, vanilla, and oak. In the mouth, flavors of crushed, toasted nuts and oak are balanced by decent acidity. Perhaps a bit too much wood influence here for me. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $450. click to buy.

2023 Domaine de Montille “Les Clous Dessous” Meursault, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers and grapefruit pith. In the mouth, zippy flavors of lemon pith, grapefruit, and crushed nuts have a zingy brightness thanks to great acidity. Tasted from magnum. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $120. click to buy.

Red Wines With a Score Between 9.5 and 10

2023 Domaine Hudelot-Noëllat Romanée-Saint-Vivant Grand Cru, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of raspberry, meat, bramble, flowers, and something coniferous, like pine. In the mouth, tangy flavors of raspberry and redcurrant continue that piney quality, giving the fruit edge and lingering through a very long, long finish. Fantastic acidity, the finest of tannins, and showing incredible complexity and length. This is a jaw-dropping wine. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $1900. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Ponsot Clos de la Roche Grand Cru, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of wildflowers, wet stones, earth, and raspberries. In the mouth, bright, pure raspberry flavors have a crystalline clarity, wrapped in fine tannins and lifted by fantastic acidity through a long finish. Soaring aromatics and electric, juicy brightness, this is a fantastically complex mouthful, with a finish that won’t quit. Made from 65-year-old vines. Score: between 9.5 and 10. Cost: $840. click to buy.

Red Wines With a Score Around 9.5

2023 Domaine Marquis d’Angerville “Fremiet Premier Cru” Volnay, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of wet stones, flowers, and a pronounced earthiness. In the mouth, tangy flavors of raspberry and earth are wrapped in powdery tannins, with a stony earthiness and great acidity. Mysterious but ever-so-refined in quality. Needs time to unfurl, but will be glorious. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $235. click to buy.

2023 Thibault Liger-Belair “Les Saint Georges Premier Cru” Nuits-Saint-Georges, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells meaty, with notes of raspberry, herbs, and flowers. In the mouth, raspberry and spice flavors are wrapped in fine tannins and lifted by great acidity. Complex and long, with gauzy tannins and beautiful aromatics. An extremely compelling wine. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $220. click to buy.

2023 Thibault Liger-Belair Richebourg Grand Cru, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells meaty, with notes of raspberry, flowers, and herbs. In the mouth, intense, tangy raspberry flavors mix with meat, dried herbs, and flowers, while great acidity carries it all into a long finish. Mouthwatering, with a hint of salinity, and sporting incredibly supple tannins. A stunner of a wine. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $1200. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Hudelot-Noëllat Vosne-Romanée, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine offers an expressive nose of pure raspberry and bright floral notes. In the mouth, tangy raspberry and floral flavors have a zippy brightness, wrapped in fine tannins that linger through a long finish. Lithe, lifted, and gorgeous, with incredible acidity and juiciness. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $145. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Hudelot-Noëllat “Les Suchots Premier Cru” Vosne-Romanée, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of raspberry, flowers, and earth. In the mouth, refined, fine, fleecy tannins wrap around bright, zippy flavors of raspberry and redcurrant. Fantastic crackling acidity and lovely floral high notes linger for a long time. Stupendous. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $330. click to buy.

2023 Domaine des Chezeaux Griotte-Chambertin Grand Cru, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet with purple highlights in the glass, this wine smells of earth, violets, and raspberries. In the mouth, bright, citrusy raspberry flavors are wrapped in mouth-coating tannins that linger intense and long through the finish. Excellent acidity and balance, with a long life ahead of it. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $760. click to buy.

2023 Domaine des Lambrays Clos des Lambrays Grand Cru, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of flowers, raspberries, and wet stones. In the mouth, deep, stony flavors of earth and raspberry are still tightly wound. This wine needs time, but its floral qualities and impeccable balance suggest it will soar eventually. Powerful. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $820. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Ponsot “Cuvée des Alouettes Premier Cru” Morey-Saint-Denis, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of flowers, plum skin, raspberry liqueur, and pine. In the mouth, tangy, bright flavors of raspberry and redcurrant have a resinous edge, wrapped in fine tannins and lifted by great acidity through a long finish. Poised, regal, and delicious. Outstanding. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $175. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Ponsot Chapelle-Chambertin Grand Cru, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of wet stones, flowers, and raspberry. In the mouth, stony, etched flavors of raspberry and redcurrant are wrapped in fine, powdery tannins, with great acidity and a long finish. Wonderfully aromatic and beautifully balanced. A stunner of a wine. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $360. click to buy.

Red Wines With a Score Between 9 and 9.5

2023 Domaine Pierre Morey “Pitures Premier Cru” Volnay, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of meat, earth, raspberry, and redcurrant. In the mouth, meaty raspberry flavors are stony and very mineral, with good acidity and a long finish. A wonderful balance between savory notes, fruit, and an underlying minerality. Beautiful. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $??

2023 Domaine Marquis d’Angerville “Clos des Angles Premier Cru” Volnay, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of earth, herbs, raspberry, and stone. In the mouth, deep flavors of stone, earth, raspberry, and dried herbs linger through the finish. Wonderfully balanced with excellent poise, great acidity, and a nice lift. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $180. click to buy.

2023 Domaine de Montille “Aux Malconsorts Premier Cru” Vosne-Romanée, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of wet stones, flowers, and earth. In the mouth, stony flavors of earth and flowers are wrapped in fleecy tannins, and linger for a long time on the palate. Excellent acidity and a wonderful floral top note make for a delicious experience. Tasted from magnum. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $650. click to buy.

2023 Domaine David Duband Échézeaux Grand Cru, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of sappy raspberry, flowers, herbs, and earth. In the mouth, flavors of raspberry, earth, and dried herbs are wrapped in fine tannins, with great acidity, a long finish, and a faint salinity that makes the experience all that more mouthwatering. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $??

2023 Thibault Liger-Belair “La Charmotte” Nuits-Saint-Georges, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of meat, raspberry, and resin. In the mouth, bright raspberry flavors mix with sappy herbs and a resinous note that lingers in a long finish. Excellent acidity and fine tannins with a wonderful tension. Delicious. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $??

2023 Thibault Liger-Belair Clos Vougeot Grand Cru, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of flowers, earth, and raspberry. In the mouth, earthy flavors of dried herbs are wrapped in fine, fleecy tannins, with great acidity. Very pretty and poised, with a somewhat broad-shouldered quality. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $??

2023 Domaine des Lambrays “La Richemone Premier Cru” Nuits-Saint-Georges, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of resin, raspberry, and citrus oil. In the mouth, flavors of raspberry, dried herbs, and redcurrant linger for a long time in the finish. Fantastic acidity and that tangy resinous quality make for an attractive, mouthwatering character. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $615. click to buy.

2023 Domaine des Lambrays “Clos Sorbè Premier Cru” Morey-Saint-Denis, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of flowers, raspberry, herbs, and earth. In the mouth, earthy flavors of dried herbs and raspberry are wrapped in fine tannins with a stony quality that lingers through the finish. Lovely acidity and great balance. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $250. click to buy.

Red Wines With a Score Around 9

2023 Domaine Bachelet-Monnot “La Fussière Premier Cru” Maranges, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France

Score: around 9. Cost: $83. click to buy.

2023 Domaine David Duband Nuits-Saint-Georges, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France

2023 Domaine David Duband “Clos Sorbè Premier Cru” Morey-Saint-Denis, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of earth and raspberry, cherry, and dried herbs. In the mouth, intense flavors of raspberry, earth, and citrus peel are driven by great acidity, while fine tannins offer a light grip. Bright and mouthwatering. Score: around 9. Cost: $140. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Amiot-Servelle “Les Charmes Premier Cru” Chambolle-Musigny, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of raspberry, flowers, and herbs. In the mouth, flavors of raspberry and redcurrant mix with dried and green herbs and a touch of oak. Faint tannins. Very good acidity. Nice balance. Score: around 9. Cost: $165. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Amiot-Servelle “Derrière la Grange Premier Cru” Chambolle-Musigny, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of earth and herbs, raspberry and a hint of leather. In the mouth, fleecy, powdery tannins wrap around flavors of raspberry and green herbs. There’s a faint rusticity here amidst the fruit and savory herbs that is charming. Very good acidity. Score: around 9. Cost: $??

2023 Domaine Amiot-Servelle “Les Amoureuses Premier Cru” Chambolle-Musigny, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of meat, flowers, and raspberry. In the mouth, earthy, stony flavors of raspberry and river mud are wrapped in fleecy tannins. Nice, juicy acidity, but with darker earth tones that linger. Score: around 9. Cost: $675. click to buy.

2023 Domaine René Bouvier “Racine du Temps” Gevrey-Chambertin, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of flowers and tangy raspberries. In the mouth, tangy raspberry flavors mix with sweet oak and dried herbs, wrapped in fine tannins through a long finish. Excellent acidity. Score: around 9. Cost: $185. click to buy.

2023 Domaine René Bouvier Charmes-Chambertin Grand Cru, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of raspberry, earth, and dried flowers. In the mouth, flavors of raspberry, earth, and dried herbs are wrapped in fine tannins, with a long finish. Excellent acidity. Score: around 9. Cost: $??

Red Wines With a Score Between 8.5 and 9

2023 Domaine Marquis d’Angerville Bourgogne Rouge, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells meaty, with notes of raspberry and cranberry. In the mouth, fine tannins wrap around tangy flavors of red berries and citrus peel with a hint of earth. Decent acidity. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $85. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Clos de la Chapelle “Clos de la Chapelle Premier Cru” Volnay, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of raspberry and citrus peel. In the mouth, flavors of citrus peel and redcurrant are taut and lean, with bright acidity and an athletic tannin profile. Very good acidity. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $165. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Clos de la Chapelle “Les Taillepieds Premier Cru” Volnay, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of wet stones, raspberry and herbs. In the mouth, green herbs, raspberry, and earth flavors remain tight and restrained by muscular tannins that need some time to relax. Very good acidity. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $165. click to buy.

2023 Domaine David Duband “Louis Auguste” Bourgogne Hautes Côtes de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Pale garnet in the glass, this wine smells of cherry and raspberry. In the mouth, sweet raspberry and green herb flavors are lifted by great acidity, and linger for a long time, wrapped in gauzy tannins. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $55. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Amiot-Servelle Chambolle-Musigny, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of raspberry, redcurrant, herbs, and bramble. In the mouth, flavors of raspberry and bramble mix with citrus peel and chopped green herbs. Light tannins, good acidity. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $125. click to buy.

2023 Domaine des Lambrays Morey-Saint-Denis, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of raspberry, citrus peel, earth, and bramble. In the mouth, flavors of raspberry and redcurrant mix with earth and dried herbs. Light tannins, very good acidity. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $140. click to buy.

2023 Domaine René Bouvier “Crais de Chêne” Fixin, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of raspberry, redcurrant, and stone. In the mouth, bright flavors of citrus peel and raspberry have a hint of oak and great acidity. Faint tannins. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $75. click to buy.

Red Wines With a Score Around 8.5

2023 Pierre Meurgey “Les Grands Epenots Premier Cru” Pommard, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of flowers and sweet oak. In the mouth, sweet, oaky raspberry flavors dominate. Simply too much oak for my taste. Decent acidity. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $146. click to buy.

2023 Domaine René Bouvier “Clos du Roy” Marsannay, Côte de Nuits, Burgundy, France
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of raspberry and herbs. In the mouth, flavors of raspberry and earth mix with dried herbs under a cottony blanket of tannins. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $60. click to buy.

The post Wine News: What I’m Reading the Week of 10/11/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly roundup of the wine stories that I find of interest on the web. I spend each week exploring the internet for everything published about wine online, and here’s all the stuff that I think would be worth your valuable time.

Masked robbers steal wine worth over $5m from top Italian vineyard
Biggest wine theft ever, say some folks. The Marchese isn’t pleased. As an aside, do you know how hard it is to steal 30,000 wine bottles?!?

Turning the Tables on Matt Kettmann
Profile of the man from Santa Barbara.

Affordable Luxury
OK, but should we even be using the “L” word for wine?

Time to Get Real
Real talk from Ted Hall. A clear-eyed post.

What if Your Neighbour Was Your Occasional Wine Merchant?
Peer-to-peer wine sales has been tried before.

Can revamping a 45-year-old winery draw visitors to a wine region in the South Bay’s ‘backyard’?
Fogarty is making better wines than it ever has.

French wine industry facing historic low harvest after extreme summer heat
Less wine everywhere, but that might be a good thing.

The one crucial thing that would make Gen Z buy fine wine
Not really answered here.

Why Is California Wine’s Correction Worsening?
Because it’s built on debt.

French v NZ – the results of a blind wine tasting might surprise you
The latest blind tasting stunt.

Mexico Moves to Certify Wine Origin as Production Grows
Such moves are almost always good for consumers.

Wine talk: All’s well that ends well
A new map of Israeli wine regions.

My favorite hidden gem in California has incredible food and wine — and it’s more affordable than Napa Valley
An ode to Paso Robles.

This Bordeaux-Style Wine Tells the Story of a Sicilian Legend
Fancy, but does the world need another expensive Cabernet-based blend?

Brazilians Reach Record Per Capita Wine Consumption
But California doesn’t give it much focus at all. That should change.

People Still Want Wine at Their Gatherings—but Gathering Is the Challenge
It’s the phones. Put down the phones.

Short Crop Won’t Be Wine’s Savior
There is no silver bullet in a market correction.

Searching for weaker wines
Not that kind of weak. Less than 13% weak.
